findings.title: reinforced negated predicate
findings.claim: The bāʾ attached to the denied participle strengthens the refusal and does not introduce spatial or instrumental meaning.
findings.mechanism: The particle follows the nominal negator and precedes bāsiṭ, binding the predicate to reinforced denial.
findings.reader_payoff: The refusal lands as categorical before the extender identity is heard.
findings.containment: This qualifies the force of the refusal; it does not erase the conditional frame or add a separate physical act.

epistemic.reason: The focus morphology and attachment evidence directly support the relation.

findings.title: predicate arrives under denial
findings.claim: The denied participle is heard as arriving already bound to reinforced negation.
findings.mechanism: The ordering of negator, bāʾ, and participle, together with the repeated b-sound, makes the predicate acoustically and syntactically dependent.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can hear the predicate enter under denial rather than as an unqualified action.
findings.containment: The sound binding is a local texture effect and does not create an additional negation or change the syntax.

epistemic.reason: Trusted sound and ordering evidence supports a real auditory payoff, while its semantic effect remains limited.

findings.title: human violent extension refused
findings.claim: The repeated b-s-t form makes the human hand-extension a refused violent identity in this ayah.
findings.mechanism: The same root returns as an indefinite active participle under negation and is governed by the hand and directional phrase.
findings.reader_payoff: The threat is carried into a named class of hand-extenders that the speaker refuses to join.
findings.containment: The broader spreading and generosity range remains contrastive lexical pressure; no charitable sense is asserted as the local predicate.

epistemic.reason: The local participial relation is grounded, while the supplied wider range is explicitly bounded.

findings.title: participle governs withheld hand
findings.claim: The participle bāsiṭ is an extender specifically of the speaker's hand toward the aggressor.
findings.mechanism: The active participle governs the possessed hand and the directional complement, so its extension is bodily and targeted rather than abstract.
findings.reader_payoff: The refused identity becomes concrete as extending a hand toward the other person.
findings.containment: The finding does not claim that every use of b-s-t is bodily or hostile; that narrowing comes from this ayah's hand and killing frame.

epistemic.reason: The focus morphology and attachment evidence directly support the relation.

findings.title: denied extender identity
findings.claim: The speaker denies membership in the class of agents who extend a hand for killing, not only one future act.
findings.mechanism: An indefinite active participle under negation functions as the predicate of the speaker's identity clause.
findings.reader_payoff: Non-retaliation is perceptible as a stated counter-identity.
findings.containment: The identity force remains within this refusal; it does not assert an unqualified claim about every future circumstance.

epistemic.reason: The focus morphology and attachment evidence directly support the relation.

findings.title: root repetition under negation
findings.claim: The threat's b-s-t root is repeated under negation in a changed participial form, turning lexical repetition into a refusal.
findings.mechanism: The finite threatened extension and the later active participle share the root, but the second occurrence is placed under the negated nominal construction.
findings.reader_payoff: The answer visibly reuses the aggressor's lexical material while reversing its force.
findings.containment: The repetition explains the local contrast; it does not make the two forms grammatically interchangeable.

epistemic.reason: The focus morphology and attachment evidence directly support the relation.

findings.title: construct and emphatic variants
findings.claim: The supplied construct and emphatic-sound variants sharpen the participle-hand relation without changing the refusal.
findings.mechanism: Variant readings alter the participial shape or its sound texture while the governing hand and negation remain constant.
findings.reader_payoff: The denied extension can sound tighter or heavier without becoming a new action.
findings.containment: Variant pressure is retained only as form and sound evidence; the main participial relation remains the boundary.

epistemic.reason: Trusted variant rows support a bounded contrast rather than an alternative local syntax.

findings.title: possessor reversal makes restraint visible
findings.claim: The repeated hand noun makes restraint visible by changing the possessor from the aggressor to the speaker.
findings.mechanism: The two singular possessed forms keep the same noun while reversing the person suffixes inside the mirrored clauses.
findings.reader_payoff: The same instrument is present on both sides, but only the speaker's hand is grammatically withheld.
findings.containment: The reversal does not mean the hands have identical agency or that the threat is repeated as an action.

epistemic.reason: The focus morphology and attachment evidence directly support the relation.

findings.title: speaker hand as agency
findings.claim: The speaker's hand carries both concrete limb and agency pressure, while the local grammar keeps it a possessed hand.
findings.mechanism: The lexical range includes hand and agency, but the participle, possession, direction, and killing purpose anchor the form in a concrete instrument.
findings.reader_payoff: Restraint is seen as undeployed capacity rather than an abstract absence of power.
findings.containment: Agency remains a bounded pressure around the bodily hand; the finding does not replace the ordinary limb reading.

epistemic.reason: The trusted range row itself narrows the broader agency field to the concrete possessed hand.

findings.title: shorter vowel variant
findings.claim: The shorter vowel variant preserves the possessed-hand relation while changing its vocalic release.
findings.mechanism: The variant touches the final sound of the first-person possessed form, but not its syntax, possessor, or role under negation.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can notice a shorter release without losing the withheld instrument.
findings.containment: This is a recitational and form-level alternative, not a different act or agent.

epistemic.reason: Trusted variant evidence changes vocalic texture while preserving the established relation.

findings.title: my hand as withheld instrument
findings.claim: The speaker's own hand is grammatically present as the instrument he deliberately does not deploy.
findings.mechanism: The first-person possessive suffix places the hand under the denied participle, so capacity is named before its lethal use is refused.
findings.reader_payoff: The ayah distinguishes restraint from helplessness.
findings.containment: The finding concerns withheld retaliation in this hand-and-killing frame; it does not claim that every use of the hand is forbidden.

epistemic.reason: The focus morphology and attachment evidence directly support the relation.

findings.title: mirror geography completed
findings.claim: The directional geography reverses exactly: the threatened movement is toward me, while the refused movement would be toward you.
findings.mechanism: The paired ilā forms carry opposite person endpoints and the second direction remains inside the negated hand-extension.
findings.reader_payoff: The two-person geometry of possible retaliation becomes visible before the motive clause closes it.
findings.containment: The mirrored directions do not make the second movement actual; it remains a refused possibility.

epistemic.reason: The focus morphology and attachment evidence directly support the relation.

findings.title: aggressor as refused endpoint
findings.claim: The aggressor is marked as the possible endpoint of retaliation, but only inside the refusal.
findings.mechanism: The second-person suffix on ilayka supplies the target of the speaker's possible movement, while negation blocks the hand-extension and its purpose.
findings.reader_payoff: The answer names exactly where retaliation could go before denying that trajectory.
findings.containment: The endpoint is grammatically projected, not enacted, and no independent threat is added.

epistemic.reason: The focus morphology and attachment evidence directly support the relation.

findings.title: matched purpose connector
findings.claim: The second purpose connector makes the speaker's refused killing purpose the structural twin of the aggressor's purpose.
findings.mechanism: The two purpose lām particles introduce parallel killing goals, while the second is governed by the negated predicate.
findings.reader_payoff: Intention itself becomes part of the audible mirror.
findings.containment: Structural parallelism does not turn the refused purpose into an independent threat.

epistemic.reason: The supplied evidence supports the relation with the boundary stated above.

findings.title: killing purpose under negation
findings.claim: The speaker's possible killing purpose is explicitly named only as what he will not do.
findings.mechanism: The second lām attaches the killing verb to the refused hand-extension, placing the purpose under negation.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader sees that the hand is refused because of its lethal end, not merely because it moves.
findings.containment: The purpose clause remains hypothetical and negated; it does not assert retaliatory action.

epistemic.reason: The focus morphology and attachment evidence directly support the relation.

findings.title: non-killing within killing field
findings.claim: The refused first-person q-t-l form remains inside the ayah's killing field while fear of God prevents it from becoming action.
findings.mechanism: The same Form I killing root carries the reversed purpose clause, but its subject and object are placed under the prior negation.
findings.reader_payoff: Killing can be named without being enacted, so the refusal does not soften the lethal endpoint.
findings.containment: The finding keeps the literal local q-t-l sense and does not import a separate combat or overpowering branch.

epistemic.reason: The trusted word analysis establishes the local q-t-l relation; the cross-ayah pressure is not needed for this bounded claim.

findings.title: person reversal in same verb
findings.claim: The same killing verb reverses subject and object, making retaliation grammatically available before it is refused.
findings.mechanism: The two q-t-l forms share purpose structure while their person marking switches from second-person subject and first-person object to the reverse.
findings.reader_payoff: The answer mirrors the threat without accepting its role.
findings.containment: The person reversal is grammatical symmetry, not a claim that the speaker actually enters the killing circuit.

epistemic.reason: The focus morphology and attachment evidence directly support the relation.

findings.title: motive blocks reciprocal killing
findings.claim: The following fear-of-God clause supplies the stated motive that blocks the mirrored killing purpose.
findings.mechanism: The refused q-t-l clause is followed by the emphatic causal disclosure beginning with innī and naming fear.
findings.reader_payoff: The ethical reason is heard as governing the refused action rather than as a detached afterthought.
findings.containment: The finding links the clauses locally; it does not infer motives beyond the supplied wording.

epistemic.reason: The focus morphology and attachment evidence directly support the relation.

findings.title: clipped refused verb texture
findings.claim: The clipped refused-verb variant changes sound shape while leaving the syntactic refusal intact.
findings.mechanism: Variant and sound evidence affects the form of the q-t-l verb, but its first-person subject, second-person object, purpose attachment, and negation remain.
findings.reader_payoff: The hard killing texture can be heard as clipped without changing who refuses what.
findings.containment: This is limited to recitation and form; it is not a second killing reading.

epistemic.reason: Trusted variant evidence supports a bounded sound contrast only.

findings.title: principle becomes motive
findings.claim: The emphatic first-person particle turns the previously stated principle into the speaker's immediate motive.
findings.mechanism: Innī opens the explanation of the refusal and anchors the causal disclosure in the same speaker.
findings.reader_payoff: The transition from mirrored human action to vertical motive becomes explicit.
findings.containment: The particle introduces the motive clause but does not by itself add a new ethical rule.

epistemic.reason: The supplied boundary row connects the focus clause to the declared preceding context.

findings.title: emphatic reason for refusal
findings.claim: The final clause is the causal ground of non-retaliation, not a detached statement.
findings.mechanism: The emphatic particle opens the clause that explains why the speaker will not extend his hand for killing.
findings.reader_payoff: Fear is perceptible as the reason for the refusal.
findings.containment: The causal relation is local to the ayah's syntax and does not rank fear above the other supplied relations.

epistemic.reason: The focus morphology and attachment evidence directly support the relation.

findings.title: speaker marker and variant release
findings.claim: The motive clause begins by re-anchoring the same first-person speaker, with the variant release making that anchoring more audible.
findings.mechanism: The particle combines first-person reference and emphasis before the fear predicate, while its variant changes vocalic release only.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader hears the person who refused the act now state his own ground.
findings.containment: The variant does not change the speaker or the causal relation.

epistemic.reason: Trusted form evidence preserves the speaker marker while limiting the variant to sound.

findings.title: taqwā enacted as fear
findings.claim: The God-conscious criterion supplied in the preceding ayah becomes personal fear that restrains this speaker here.
findings.mechanism: The imperfect fear verb is placed in the motive clause after the refusal, creating a local boundary from principle to enacted restraint.
findings.reader_payoff: A general criterion becomes an immediate first-person practice.
findings.containment: The finding uses only the declared 5:27 boundary and does not claim a surah-wide system.

epistemic.reason: The focus morphology and attachment evidence directly support the relation.

branch_activations.branch_gloss: bir belirtiye dayanarak kötü bir şey bekleme korkusu
branch_activations.facet_statement: İstenmeyen bir olayın gerçekleşeceği, bilinen ya da sanılan bir belirtiye dayanılarak beklenir.
branch_activations.carrier: The kh-w-f form carries expectation of an adverse consequence and the fear it produces.
branch_activations.independent_trigger: Its direct Allah object and the emphatic motive-clause marker independently make the fear God-directed and causal.
branch_activations.activation: Fear contacts the divine object as the reason the hand is withheld.
branch_activations.resulting_reading: The fear branch colors the local ethical restraint without replacing the ordinary fear verb.
branch_activations.boundary: No fear-causing or external fear branch is asserted.

findings.title: fear redirected to Allah
findings.claim: Fear is directed to Allah rather than to the aggressor, death, or retaliation.
findings.mechanism: The imperfect kh-w-f verb directly governs the divine name as its object, redirecting the axis of the scene.
findings.reader_payoff: The reason for restraint moves vertically beyond the two-person conflict.
findings.containment: The finding identifies the supplied object relation; it does not deny that the threat itself is dangerous.

epistemic.reason: The focus morphology and attachment evidence directly support the relation.

findings.title: ongoing ethical restraint
findings.claim: The imperfect fear form presents God-directed restraint as an ongoing orientation rather than momentary panic.
findings.mechanism: The imperfect aspect and its placement as the motive of refusal connect continued fear with continued non-retaliation.
findings.reader_payoff: Fear becomes a durable ethical brake on the hand.
findings.containment: Ongoing orientation is a form-level and local reading, not a claim about every psychological state.

epistemic.reason: The focus morphology and attachment evidence directly support the relation.

findings.title: sound separates motive clause
findings.claim: The fear verb breaks from the stop-heavy killing texture into a distinct motive sound.
findings.mechanism: The supplied phonetic row identifies a concrete cadence change at the start of the final clause.
findings.reader_payoff: The close sounds like a change of register after the harder threat and refusal.
findings.containment: Sound contrast colors the motive clause but does not establish a new semantic branch.

epistemic.reason: Trusted sound evidence gives a local auditory payoff with limited semantic reach.

findings.title: same divine referent across boundary
findings.claim: Allah is the definite direct object of fear and the starting point of the closing divine designation.
findings.mechanism: The accusative proper name is governed by kh-w-f, while the following appositional title expands its reference.
findings.reader_payoff: The motive is fixed on the divine referent rather than on the brother or death.
findings.containment: The lexical background of deity and devotion remains bounded pressure; the local grammar selects the feared divine referent.

epistemic.reason: The focus morphology and attachment evidence directly support the relation.

branch_activations.branch_gloss: Yaratıcıya özgü ad ile seslenme ve ant biçimleri
branch_activations.facet_statement: Dalın merkezinde, Yaratıcıyı başkalarından ayırarak gösteren ve yalnız ona özgü sayılan özel ad bulunur.
branch_activations.carrier: The proper divine-name form carries the focus's Yaratıcıya özgü ad.
branch_activations.independent_trigger: The fear relation and appositional Rabb title independently identify the name's local referent and function.
branch_activations.activation: The name is contacted by both the motive predicate and the closing title, activating its proper-name core.
branch_activations.resulting_reading: The branch adds name-specific force to the direct object without making it a generic deity noun.
branch_activations.boundary: The associated oath and invocation facets are not activated.

findings.title: name expands into universal title
findings.claim: The close builds from fear to the divine name, then to a title and universal scope.
findings.mechanism: Apposition and the following construct connect the name to Rabb and al-ʿālamīn as one expanding designation.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can follow the closing enlargement instead of receiving the title as a separate object.
findings.containment: The sequence describes the local closure and does not claim a wider architecture.

epistemic.reason: The focus morphology and attachment evidence directly support the relation.

findings.title: definite object of fear
findings.claim: The divine name is the grammatical object of fear, not the brother, death, or retaliation.
findings.mechanism: The accusative proper noun is directly governed by the fear verb before the appositional title specifies it.
findings.reader_payoff: The source of restraint is syntactically unambiguous.
findings.containment: This is a local object relation; it does not settle every derivational association of the divine name.

epistemic.reason: The focus morphology and attachment evidence directly support the relation.

findings.title: worshipful divine name range
findings.claim: The divine name carries a bounded pressure of deity, worship, refuge, and awe while its local role remains the feared referent.
findings.mechanism: The root range supplies semantic background, but the proper-name form and accusative syntax constrain the reading here.
findings.reader_payoff: The name is felt as more than an empty label without replacing its direct-object function.
findings.containment: The range does not turn the proper name into a generic word for every worshiped entity.

epistemic.reason: The trusted range row explicitly preserves semantic pressure while retaining the local proper-name role.

findings.title: recognized universal formula
findings.claim: Rabb binds the feared name to a recognized title whose scope reaches the worlds.
findings.mechanism: The appositional title and construct relation connect the local name to al-ʿālamīn, with the supplied 1:2 formula as a declared comparison.
findings.reader_payoff: Lordship generalizes the motive beyond the two persons in conflict.
findings.containment: The formula is a local contact with the declared Fātiḥa context, not a surah-wide thesis.

epistemic.reason: The focus morphology and attachment evidence directly support the relation.

findings.title: title apposes the name
findings.claim: Rabb apposes the divine name and specifies the same feared referent rather than introducing a second object.
findings.mechanism: Its accusative appositional position and construct link to the final plural make the title grammatically dependent on the name.
findings.reader_payoff: The closing title clarifies whom the speaker fears.
findings.containment: The title's relation is grammatical and local; it does not split the closing into separate divine referents.

epistemic.reason: The focus morphology and attachment evidence directly support the relation.

findings.title: nurturing owner and completer
findings.claim: Rabb carries a bounded pressure of owning, tending, sustaining, and bringing to completion within the appositional title.
findings.mechanism: The root range colors the title, while its local syntax keeps it attached to Allah and completed by the worlds.
findings.reader_payoff: The motive for preserving life is heard under a title of governance and care.
findings.containment: These are lexical facets around the title, not a claim that every Rabb branch is activated here.

epistemic.reason: The trusted range evidence preserves the broader pressure while the appositional grammar supplies the boundary.

branch_activations.facet_statement: Sahiplik, buyruk yetkisi ve yönetip düzenleme aynı çekirdekte birleşir.
branch_activations.carrier: The Rabb form carries owning, governing, and ordering authority.
branch_activations.independent_trigger: The divine name and the following universal construct complement independently frame the title.
branch_activations.activation: The apposition contacts lordship with both the feared referent and its comprehensive domain.
branch_activations.resulting_reading: The title is heard as governance over the named worlds in this closing clause.
branch_activations.boundary: The broader nurture and completion pressure remains bounded lexical color here.

findings.title: compact title before expansion
findings.claim: The compact title is heard before the final word opens the cadence into a wider plural.
findings.mechanism: The supplied sound row contrasts the doubled compact form of Rabb with the longer final expansion.
findings.reader_payoff: The closing moves audibly from concentrated title to broadened scope.
findings.containment: This is a cadence effect and does not alter the appositional construction.

epistemic.reason: Trusted phonetic evidence supports the local cadence contrast.

findings.title: continued direct speech boundary
findings.claim: The ayah continues the accepted brother's direct speech from 5:27 into a solemn confrontation.
